newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Herzog pledges Bonn's support for Czech EU entry.
newsitem.headline: Herzog pledges Bonn's support for Czech EU entry.

text.p: German President Roman Herzog expressed regret on Thursday for the pain and injustice inflicted on the Czechs by Nazi conquest and occupation, and said they could count on Bonn's support in their attempt to join the European Union and NATO.

Herzog, in the latest act of post-war reconciliation between the two states, told both houses of the Prague parliament that it was Germany's war-time actions which led to the post-war expulsion of Germans from Czech territory.

"We regret the suffering and injustice which was caused to the Czech people and we are aware that only this policy of violence and crime prepared the ground for the subsequent flight and expulsion," Herzog said, to applause.

Telling deputies that nations could only secure their future by working together, Herzog pledged Bonn's support for Czech efforts to join both the EU and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
"We welcome the Czech Republic into the European Union. You can count on full German support," he said.
Herzog's speech in the historic Vladislav Hall of Prague Castle followed a similar address last week by Czech President Vaclav Havel to the German parliament.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus signed in January a joint declaration, drawn up after two years of tortuous negotiations, which was designed to heal the wounds left by World War Two.

In the accord, Bonn expresses its regret for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague its sorrow for brutality in the post-war expulsion of some 1.5 million ethnic Germans from Czech territory.
"We Germans want to ask for forgiveness and we want to forgive," Herzog said, echoing a similar statement by Kohl in Prague in January.
The accord was designed to forge the same untroubled relations Germany has with other of its neighbours and was seen as an essential pre-condition to the Czechs joining both the EU and NATO.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are the leading candidates to be the first new members of both groups and Herzog said Europe without them would be incomplete.

The declaration has proved highly controversial in both countries. Friends and supporters of the expelled Sudeten Germans say the accord should have addressed their claims to confiscated property while some Czechs have said it does not make explicit that the Czech actions were legally based.
Acknowledging that bitter feelings existed on both sides, Herzog said most Germans wanted to be good neighbours.
"Citizens of the Czech Republic can be convinced that the vast majority of Germans and of Sudeten Germans want reconciliation and to be good neighbours with you," he said.
Deputies from the far-right Republican Party, who regard the declaration as treachery, boycotted the speech, which received a standing ovation.
